draft.subject: Article suitability: comparing shell models and configurations with Elementa
draft.message:
I'm Michael Smolkin, the developer of Elementa, a free chemistry study website. I'm writing in that role, not as an independent reviewer of the product.

Would a practical Article about comparing simplified shell models with ground-state electron configurations fit ChemEd X? The proposed walkthrough would use oxygen and sulfur to connect their configurations, occupied shells and positions in the periodic table, explain the limits of the diagrams, and include a short example worksheet with an answer key. Elementa provides 118 reference pages, comparisons and short quizzes without signup. I would cite the underlying chemistry references and identify the website as my own work.

I don't have classroom-trial or learning-outcome evidence to report. Please advise whether this approach fits an Article or whether an independent instructor's evaluation would be more useful.

draft.name: Elementa
draft.tagline: Explore 118 elements, compare properties, and practice
draft.description: A free chemistry study website with 118 element pages, comparisons, simplified shell/orbital views, short quizzes, and printable worksheets with answer keys. No signup; notes and progress stay in your browser.
draft.maker_comment:
I'm Michael Smolkin, the developer of Elementa. It brings element reference pages, comparisons and short practice sessions into one browser-based tool.

You can look up an element, inspect its simplified shell/orbital view, compare it with another element, then try a quiz or print a worksheet with an answer key. Quizzes currently have up to five questions; single-element practice uses four distinct concepts. Notes and progress stay in the browser, with export/import for backups.

It's free and doesn't require signup. I'd like feedback from people studying or teaching introductory chemistry: which explanation or question would you change after trying it?
